title: Heaps
description: Understand binary heaps, heap operations, and how they power priority queues and efficient sorting.

data.text: A heap is a specialized tree that satisfies the heap property: in a max-heap, every parent is greater than or equal to its children; in a min-heap, every parent is less than or equal to its children. Because the extreme value always sits at the root, heaps are ideal for priority queues and for building efficient sorting algorithms.

A binary heap is usually stored in an array. For a node at index i, its left child sits at 2i + 1 and its right child at 2i + 2. This compact layout avoids pointer overhead and keeps the heap cache-friendly.

data.title: Array representation of a max-heap
data.content: The max-heap [90, 70, 60, 50, 40] stored as an array satisfies the heap property because every parent is larger than its children.

data.title: Heap operations and their costs
items: insert: add at the end, then bubble up to restore the heap property — O(log n).
extract max or min: swap root with the last element, remove it, then bubble down — O(log n).
peek: look at the root — O(1).
heapify: build a heap from an unordered array in O(n).

data.title: Heapsort trade-off
data.text: Heapsort guarantees O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space, but it is not stable. If you need a stable sort, use merge sort or Timsort instead.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Heaps are complete binary trees stored in arrays.
Insert and extract run in O(log n).
Heaps power priority queues and efficient selection algorithms.
Heapsort is fast and in-place but not stable.
data.takeaway: Heaps are the right choice whenever you need quick access to the most important item in a changing collection.
